items.content_html:
open-webui v0.6.33 is vulnerable to Incorrect Access Control. The API /api/tasks/stop/ directly accesses and cancels tasks without verifying user ownership, enabling attackers (a normal user) to stop arbitrary LLM response tasks.

items.content_html:
In version v0.3.8 of open-webui/open-webui, sensitive actions such as deleting and resetting are performed using the GET method. This vulnerability allows an attacker to perform Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks, where an unaware user can unintentionally perform sensitive actions by simply visiting a malicious site or through top-level navigation. The affected endpoints include /rag/api/v1/reset, /rag/api/v1/reset/db, /api/v1/memories/reset, and /rag/api/v1/reset/uploads. This impacts both the availability and integrity of the application.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-7035

items.content_html:
An improper access control vulnerability in open-webui/open-webui v0.3.8 allows attackers to view and delete any files. The application does not verify whether the attacker is an administrator, allowing the attacker to directly call the GET /api/v1/files/ interface to retrieve information on all files uploaded by users, which includes the ID values. The attacker can then use the GET /api/v1/files/{file_id} interface to obtain information on any file and the DELETE /api/v1/files/{file_id} interface to delete any file.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-7043

items.content_html:
Summary

When django-filer's optional per-folder permission system is enabled (FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS=True), the "Delete files and/or folders" admin action does not enforce per-folder edit permissions the way every other mutating action does. A staff user who is scoped read-only on a folder via FolderPermission (can_edit = DENY), but who holds the global Django model-level delete_* permission, can delete files and entire subfolders inside that folder — even though their move, rename, copy, and resize actions on the same folder are correctly denied.

This is an integrity / edit-control gap (unauthorized deletion). It is not a read-confidentiality issue: filer files are world-downloadable by design, so no confidentiality claim is made.

Affected versions

  • django-filer <= 3.4.4 (verified end-to-end on 3.4.4 and on master prior to the fix).

Only installations running with FILER_ENABLE_PERMISSIONS = True (the optional per-folder FolderPermission system) are affected. Deployments that leave permissions disabled (the default) rely solely on Django model-level permissions and are not impacted by this specific gap.

Patched versions

  • Fixed in PR #1605. Upgrade to the first release containing that commit (3.5.0 or later).

Details

The delete_files_or_folders admin action in filer/admin/folderadmin.py authorized deletion using only:

  1. self.has_delete_permission(request) — which returns True for obj=None, and
  2. the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission (enforced downstream by the admin delete machinery).

It never called check_folder_edit_permissions or check_files_edit_permissions. Every sibling mutating action — move, rename, copy, resize — does call these helpers, which walk the selected objects (and their descendants) and enforce the per-folder can_edit grant from FolderPermission.

Because FolderPermission has no dedicated can_delete field, deletion is treated as an edit/management operation and is gated elsewhere on can_edit. The delete action's omission therefore let a folder-scoped read-only user bypass the per-folder control that constrains all their other write operations.

Precondition

The attacker must hold the Django model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission. A purely read-only user (no model-level delete perm) receives 403 and cannot exploit this. This precondition matches the standard folder-scoped-staff deployment model, where staff hold model-level permissions and are further constrained per-folder by FolderPermission.

Mitigation

  • Upgrade to the patched release.
  • Until upgrading, avoid granting the model-level delete_file / delete_folder / delete_image permission to staff who are meant to be read-only on specific folders via FolderPermission.

Credit

Reported through coordinated disclosure. Fixed in PR #1605.

References

  • https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/security/advisories/GHSA-vf85-8ff2-3r9w
  • https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/pull/1605
  • https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/commit/29d20ec0de13d7f77fa2cea93166f8d50a3f508d
  • https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/commit/742ba4c3094dd75e586ca3a05e6ad2703de4553b
  • https://github.com/django-cms/django-filer/releases/tag/3.5.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf85-8ff2-3r9w
items.title: [django-filer] django-filer: Missing per-object authorization on `discard` and `edit_redirect` version transitions

items.content_html:
Summary

The discard and edit_redirect version transitions did not enforce a per-object change-permission check, while the sibling transitions (archive, publish, unpublish, revert) all did. As a result a low-privileged staff user could discard (delete) any draft version — and thereby the underlying content object — of content they have no change permission on, and could create an editable draft off any published version, by supplying a version primary key they should not have access to (an insecure direct object reference).

Details

Version state transitions are guarded by Conditions objects declared on djangocms_versioning.models.Version. Every transition that mutates content carries the user_can_change condition, which delegates to the content object's own permission check (Version.has_change_permission → content.has_change_permission / has_placeholder_change_permission, with a final fallback to the Django change_<model> permission).

Two conditions were missing that check:

# Before (vulnerable)
check_discard = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),
    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),
])
check_edit_redirect = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),
    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),
])

The corresponding admin views authorize only through these conditions:

  • VersionAdmin.discard_view / VersionAdmin.edit_redirect_view fetch the target with the stock ModelAdmin.get_object, which is backed by the unfiltered default queryset — no per-user or per-grouper scoping.
  • The views are registered with admin_site.admin_view, which enforces only is_staff.
  • discard_view deletes the version directly via version.delete() and never consults VersionAdmin.has_delete_permission (which otherwise delegates to the content admin and honors ALLOW_DELETING_VERSIONS).

Because the only per-object gate for these two operations was the Conditions list, and that list omitted user_can_change, any staff user could invoke the operation on any version by its primary key. The changelist action buttons are disabled in the UI via check_discard.as_bool / check_edit_redirect.as_bool, but that is a client-side affordance only and does not protect the directly reachable admin URLs.

Impact

  • Type: Broken access control / missing authorization (IDOR).
  • Who is affected: Multi-editor deployments where staff users hold differentiated per-object permissions.
    • Under CMS_PERMISSION = True, authorization for these two operations was effectively reduced to is_staff, so any staff user could discard or edit-redirect any version.
    • Under the default CMS_PERMISSION = False, it degrades to the global change_<model> permission (e.g. cms.change_page) — weaker than the intended per-object check, but not absent.
  • Consequence: Unauthorized deletion of draft versions and their content objects (integrity/availability of content), and unauthorized creation of drafts from published content.

Patches

Fixed by adding the user_can_change condition to both check_discard and check_edit_redirect, restoring parity with the other content-mutating transitions:

# After (fixed)
check_discard = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT], not_draft_error),
    user_can_change(change_permission_error),
    is_not_locked(lock_error_message),
])
check_edit_redirect = Conditions([
    in_state([constants.DRAFT, constants.PUBLISHED], _("Version is not in draft or published state")),
    user_can_change(change_permission_error),
    draft_is_not_locked(lock_draft_error_message),
])

discard intentionally requires change permission (not delete): it is treated as undoing changes to a draft.

Upgrade to djangocms-versioning 2.6.1 or later.

Workarounds

There is no configuration-only workaround. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately should restrict staff accounts to trusted users, since the missing gate reduces to is_staff under CMS_PERMISSION = True.

References

  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/security/advisories/GHSA-5g9x-qwh5-33x4
  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/pull/573
  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/commit/d8c570daa5f7805e8be51f15545fe77b24c44daf
  • https://github.com/django-cms/djangocms-versioning/releases/tag/2.6.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5g9x-qwh5-33x4

items.content_html:
Vulnerable MobSF Versions: <= v4.3.2

Details: MobSF is a widely adopted mobile application security testing tool used by security teams across numerous organizations. Typically, MobSF is deployed on centralized internal or cloud-based servers that also host other security tools and web applications. Access to the MobSF web interface is often granted to internal security teams, audit teams, and external vendors.

MobSF provides a feature that allows users to upload ZIP files for static analysis. Upon upload, these ZIP files are automatically extracted and stored within the MobSF directory. However, this functionality lacks a check on the total uncompressed size of the ZIP file, making it vulnerable to a ZIP of Death (zip bomb) attack.

Due to the absence of safeguards against oversized extractions, an attacker can craft a specially prepared ZIP file that is small in compressed form but expands to a massive size upon extraction. Exploiting this, an attacker can exhaust the server's disk space, leading to a complete denial of service (DoS) not just for MobSF, but also for any other applications or websites hosted on the same server.

Attack Scenario: Suppose the server hosting MobSF has 5 GB of free disk space..

A malicious user will first create a genuine hello world application code using android studio and inside this code directory (app//src/main/java/APK_PATH/bomb.txt) he'll place a bomb.txt file.

This bomb.txt file will have billions of zeros to increase the file size on storage and make it to 4.99 GB. Now suppose the resultant hello world code directory including original code and bomb.txt files will be of 5GB, so the attacker will compress the entire hello world code directory to zip and resultant zip will be around 12-15 MBs only.

An attacker will upload this zip bomb using the MobSF web interface or API. So an attacker will spend only 12-15 MB of his bandwidth.

Now the MobSF tool will extract that zip file and it'll be automatically converted into its original size 5GB.

So now a web server will be forced to store 5GB of data and its storage will be exhausted by an attacker's single request.

Web server's storage and resources will not be able to handle other running websites or applications as the storage is exhausted. This way an attacker can achieve complete Web Server Resource Exhaustion.

Impact:

  1. This vulnerability can lead to complete server disruption in an organization which can affect other internal portals and tools too (which are hosted on the same server).
  2. If some organization has created their customised cloud based mobile security tool using MobSF core then an attacker can exploit this vulnerability to crash their servers.

POC:

  1. Screen Recording :
    https://drive.google.com/file/d/1x7GEPJr2T04Ij5ZFQQtGWvUWXtM4M4aw/view?usp=sharing
  2. POC Zip Bomb File (Upon extraction this file will consume 6GB of storage) : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1N3apL1ySMecnt3HUQcDcuH7hsjPrdwUj/view?usp=sharing

Mitigation: It is recommended to implement a safeguard that checks the total uncompressed size of any uploaded ZIP file before extraction. If the estimated uncompressed size exceeds a safe threshold (e.g., 100 MB), MobSF should reject the file and notify the user.

References

  • https://github.com/MobSF/Mobile-Security-Framework-MobSF/security/advisories/GHSA-c5vg-26p8-q8cr
  • https://github.com/MobSF/Mobile-Security-Framework-MobSF/commit/6987a946485a795f4fd38cebdb4860b368a1995d
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-46730
  • https://github.com/MobSF/Mobile-Security-Framework-MobSF
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c5vg-26p8-q8cr
  • https://github.com/pypa/advisory-database/tree/main/vulns/mobsf/PYSEC-2026-1671.yaml
  • https://pypi.org/project/mobsf

items.content_html:
Details

When the server acts as the fee_payer, pympp 0.8.0 validates calldata using eth_abi decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The FeePayerPolicy caps gas_limit (≤ 2 M) and max_fee_per_gas (≤ 100 Gwei) but does not check calldata length.

Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: 16 gas per non-zero byte. Appending N bytes of 0x01 padding inflates actual gas used by N × 16 while keeping gas_limit and max_fee_per_gas within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet.

Vulnerable code path: FeePayerPolicy in fee_payer_policy.py (pympp 0.8.0) enforces maxGas = 2_000_000 and maxFeePerGas = 100 Gwei but has no calldata.length bound. The policy check passes because the inflated gas comes from intrinsic calldata cost, not the declared gas_limit.

Note: In our experiment, we enforce an 16 KB max_header_length, which caps the maximum effective padding at roughly 5,500 bytes. The default padding in this PoC (5,500 bytes) is within that limit.

PoC

The PoC is provided below. It is configured to reproduce the attack on Tempo Moderate testnet within a Docker environment. Download the PoC and run:

unzip pympp_python_PoC.zip
cd pympp_python
docker build -t pympp-padding .
docker run --rm pympp-padding

There are more details in pympp_python/README.md

Impact

In our experiment, a malicious client can force the server to pay ~5x the normal transaction fee. This dramatically increases operational costs and completely destroys the profit margin on low-cost items.

Please provide a way to share the PoC in .zip format to you. Thank you!

References

  • https://github.com/tempoxyz/pympp/security/advisories/GHSA-v858-xh7w-8jr5
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63634
  • https://github.com/tempoxyz/pympp/commit/57a750d0d980b8e6c3bea62a40b7621f176ff1f0
  • https://github.com/tempoxyz/pympp/releases/tag/v0.9.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v858-xh7w-8jr5

items.content_html:
• Summary

A format string injection vulnerability in the applyChatTemplate GraphQL endpoint allows an attacker to read server-side environment variables, cryptographic secrets, and internal module attributes directly from the API response. On default Phoenix installations where authentication is disabled the endpoint is reachable with no credentials. On auth-enabled deployments, any account regardless of privilege level is sufficient to exploit it.

  • Impact Server filesystem paths, loaded Python module names, and internal configuration constants are fully disclosed, an attacker with network access can read the full server os.environ including the admin credentials hardcoded in phoenix.auth.

Successful exploitation allows an attacker to extract PHOENIX_SECRET, the master key used to sign all JWTs and derive the Fernet encryption key protecting stored credentials (LLM API keys, OAuth tokens). With this key, an attacker can forge admin-level session tokens and decrypt all secrets stored in the database.

  • Affected Versions

First vulnerable release: arize-phoenix-v13.0.0 (2026-02-13) Latest confirmed vulnerable release: arize-phoenix-v14.8.0 (2026-04-17)

  • Affected Component applyChatTemplate GraphQL query endpoint (src/phoenix/server/api/queries.py:1638) FStringTemplateFormatter._format() template rendering function (src/phoenix/utilities/template_formatters.py:272) DotDict.__getattr__() ineffective attribute access control (src/phoenix/utilities/template_formatters.py:90)

  • Proof of Concept payload as txt with an image performing the exploit below.

  • Payload:

{
  "query": "query($t: PromptChatTemplateInput!, $o: PromptTemplateOptions!) { applyChatTemplate(template: $t, templateOptions: $o) { messages { content { ... on TextContentPart { text { text } } } } } }",
  "variables": {
    "t": { "messages": [{ "role": "USER", "content": [{ "text": { "text": "{u.__class__.__bases__[0].__init__.__globals__[_os].environ}" } }] }] },
    "o": { "format": "F_STRING", "variables": { "u": { "x": 1 } } }
  }
}
  • Suggested Fix

Three mitigations are recommended in combination: restrict attribute traversal at the Formatter.get_field() level (not the wrapper class), add IsAuthenticated permission to the applyChatTemplate resolver, and limit F_STRING format to trusted system-defined templates only.

Best Regards, Omar

References

  • https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix/security/advisories/GHSA-gfv3-m769-5xm3
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53998
  • https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix/pull/13197
  • https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix/commit/e7224a685589f2ffae1fefcc68ff210bd6ad28b8
  • https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix/releases/tag/arize-phoenix-v15.7.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gfv3-m769-5xm3

items.content_html:
Chainlit versions prior to 2.9.4 contain an arbitrary file read vulnerability in the /project/element update flow. An authenticated client can send a custom Element with a user-controlled path value, causing the server to copy the referenced file into the attacker’s session. The resulting element identifier (chainlitKey) can then be used to retrieve the file contents via /project/file/, allowing disclosure of any file readable by the Chainlit service.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-22218
  • https://github.com/Chainlit/chainlit/releases/tag/2.9.4
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/chainlit-arbitrary-file-read-via-project-element
  • https://www.zafran.io/resources/chainleak-critical-ai-framework-vulnerabilities-expose-data-enable-cloud-takeover
  • https://github.com/Chainlit/chainlit/pull/2737

items.content_html:
Impact

write_attachments() called _safe_attachment_filename() and write_sample() inside its loop with no guard, so a single crafted attachment raised out of the whole save. Every attachment after the malicious one was silently never written, with no error surfaced to a caller that catches only MailParserError.

That is an evasion primitive as much as an availability bug: a sender puts one poisoned part first and the real payload second, and the payload never reaches the extraction directory that a downstream scanner or sandbox reads — while it still reaches the recipient's mail client intact. The tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, which is the same failure mode as the filename-sanitizing bypass in GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496.

Three shapes were reachable, all from attacker-controlled MIME metadata:

  • NUL smuggled through RFC 2231 — filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin decodes to a NUL in the filename during parsing and raised ValueError out of the name check;
  • overlong basename — a filename longer than NAME_MAX (e.g. 300 characters) raised OSError: File name too long from open(), after creating a zero-byte stub on disk;
  • undecodable payload — a body that is not valid base64 raised binascii.Error (a ValueError subclass) from the decode performed inside the open() block.
import tempfile, mailparser

raw = ("Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=b\r\n\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin\r\n\r\nxx\r\n"
       "--b\r\nContent-Type: application/octet-stream\r\n"
       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=good.bin\r\n\r\nyy\r\n"
       "--b--\r\n")

mp = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)     # parse itself is fine; safe_filename is None
mp.write_attachments(tempfile.mkdtemp())
# 4.6.0 - 4.6.2 -> ValueError, and good.bin is never written
# 4.6.3         -> logs "Skipped attachment with invalid filename: 'evil\x00.bin'";
#                  good.bin is written

parse() itself was never affected — it catches the ValueError — so only the write path was unguarded. The reject-paths that made this reachable were introduced with the filename sanitizing in 4.6.0 (PR #165).

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.3. write_attachments() now logs and skips a single unusable attachment instead of aborting the batch:

  • an invalid filename is caught and skipped;
  • overlong basenames are truncated to 240 UTF-8 bytes, preserving the extension, rather than reaching open();
  • the base64 decode moved before open(), so a failure leaves no zero-byte stub, and it now repairs padding and alphabet errors the way mail clients do (matching MIME::Base64 on 2008 cases) — rejecting them let a sender append one character to make an attachment vanish from the extraction directory while it still reached the recipient;
  • MailParserPathError is deliberately not caught by the per-attachment handler: a containment failure is not a per-attachment problem, and path-containment checks now raise MailParserPathError instead of ValueError so the broader catch cannot swallow them.

Deduplication was hardened in the same change: it reserves room for its own suffix marker (write_sample() sanitizes again, and the clamp there used to cut the marker back off, collapsing distinct attachments onto one file), resumes from the last used suffix per stem instead of rescanning from 1 (quadratic before — 16000 same-named attachments took 14 s, now milliseconds), and folds case, because APFS, exFAT and SMB collapse Invoice.pdf and invoice.pdf.

Workarounds

Upgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, do not call write_attachments() on untrusted mail; iterate parser.attachments yourself and write each attachment inside its own try/except Exception, skipping the ones whose safe_filename is None.

References

  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-8cgq-x343-p74c
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129301
  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/171
  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/11b894a0b8b3f11055a99caff118206138d1daba
  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/e1d9fe6778045d6e2c44406bc8822e3464c1097f
  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/releases/tag/4.6.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8cgq-x343-p74c
items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: One hostile attachment aborts `write_attachments()` and silently drops the rest of the batch

items.content_html:
Impact

A Received header whose trailing date carries an out-of-range year, or a timezone offset large enough to push the timestamp past the int64 epoch range, raises an exception that is outside the MailParser* hierarchy. A caller that catches only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issue as GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf, which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).

All entry points are affected: parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes(), parse_from_file(), parse_from_file_obj() and the mail-parser CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled and a single line is enough, so any pipeline that parses untrusted mail can be made to lose the message — and, if one worker handles a queue, to drop the batch.

import mailparser

raw = ("Received: from x ([1.2.3.4]) by mx.victim.com; "
       "Tue, 7 Mar 292277026596 14:29:24 +0000\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mailparser.parse_from_string(raw).mail_json
# <= 4.6.2 -> OverflowError: signed integer is greater than maximum
# 4.6.3    -> parses; the unusable hop date is reported as "date_utc": null

Root cause. receiveds_format() in src/mailparser/utils.py guarded the date conversion with except (TypeError, ValueError), but convert_mail_date() → email.utils.mktime_tz() → calendar.timegm() raises OverflowError for years whose epoch seconds overflow int64, and datetime.fromtimestamp() reports EOVERFLOW as OSError for a sufficiently large timezone offset. The date and timezone properties already wrapped the same conversion in except Exception; only the Received path was left open.

Affected range. Introduced by the date-handling change in ca2aa6a, first released in 3.7.0. Reproduced on PyPI 3.7.0, 3.8.0, 3.9.3, 4.0.0, 4.5.0, 4.6.0, 4.6.2 and on master before the fix (Python 3.14). 3.6.0 is not affected.

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.3. receiveds_format() now also catches OverflowError and OSError and records date_utc = None for that hop, so the rest of the message still parses:

try:
    j["date_utc"], _ = convert_mail_date(i["date"])
except (TypeError, ValueError, OverflowError, OSError):
    j["date_utc"] = None

A sweep of year magnitudes from 10^7 to 10^12 shows only ValueError, OverflowError and OSError are reachable on this path.

Workarounds

Upgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, wrap every parse_from_* call in a bare except Exception rather than except MailParserError, and treat the message as unparsed.

items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Uncaught `OverflowError` / `OSError` on an out-of-range `Received` date

items.content_html:
Impact

Two effects, sharing the root cause of Advisory 1 — header names chosen by the sender were resolved through Python attribute lookup and rewritten before lookup.

Uncaught exceptions. A crafted message raises an exception that is outside the MailParser* hierarchy, so a caller catching only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it and the worker dies.

Header named after a method (CWE-248, reported by @iam-niranjan). Python resolves real class attributes before __getattr__, so a header named after a method put a bound method object into the parsed mail dict. A 12-byte email is sufficient. Nine colliding names were confirmed: Parse, Message, Write_Attachments, From_File, From_File_Obj, From_File_Msg, From_String, From_Bytes, Get_Server_Ipaddress. Also reproducible from the CLI (mail-parser -f evil.eml -j).

import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_string("Parse: x\r\n\r\n").mail_json
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type method is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> {"parse": "x", "has_defects": false}

Header carrying 8-bit bytes (CWE-248). For a header containing raw 8-bit bytes, Python's compat32 policy returns an email.header.Header rather than a str, which the _raw accessor passed straight to json.dumps. This fires on entirely benign non-ASCII mail via parse_from_bytes(), the normal entry point for mail off the wire.

import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_bytes(b"Subject: caf\xe9\r\n\r\nbody\r\n").subject_raw
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type Header is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> '["caf�"]'

Silent loss of message content (CWE-436). A sender can make a header's value vanish from every output surface, or be replaced by a different header's value, with has_defects remaining false. This is an evasion primitive: the tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, and a pipeline scanning parsed output for indicators sees nothing and no failure signal.

Header names were normalised before lookup — underscores folded to dashes, and _json / _raw suffixes interpreted — so a header genuinely named Subject_json was reported with the value of Subject and its own value discarded, and any header whose name contains an underscore resolved to nothing.

import mailparser

raw = ("From: Real Sender <real@good.example>\r\n"
       "Subject: innocuous\r\n"
       "Subject_json: MALWARE-C2 http://evil.example/payload.exe\r\n"
       "X_Spam_Flag: YES\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)
print(mail.mail["subject_json"])       # 4.6.1 -> '"innocuous"'   4.6.2 -> the real value
print(mail.headers["X_Spam_Flag"])     # 4.6.1 -> ''              4.6.2 -> 'YES'
print("MALWARE-C2" in mail.mail_json)  # 4.6.1 -> False           4.6.2 -> True
print(mail.has_defects)                # both  -> False

A related case: email.message.Message.__len__ returns the header count, so a message with no headers is falsy. parse() returned before initialising state, and the unset attributes were then absorbed by __getattr__ and answered as absent headers. Every property returned '' — including mail and attachments, which are documented to return a dict and a list — with no error and no defect flag.

import mailparser
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string("Click http://evil.example/pay.exe now\r\n")
print(repr(mail.body))         # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> the text
print(repr(mail.attachments))  # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> []
print(mail.has_defects)        # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> True

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.2. Upgrade with pip install --upgrade mail-parser.

Header names taken from a message are now looked up literally — no attribute access, no case or separator folding, no suffix interpretation — so no header name can collide with a method or property, and no value can be substituted or dropped. 8-bit values are coerced to str before serialisation. Parser state is initialised before the message check, which now tests is None, and attribute names beginning with _ raise AttributeError instead of being answered as headers.

Behaviour changes. Header names now appear in mail and headers exactly as sent, so a header named X_Spam_Flag keeps that name and its own value. X_raw always returns a JSON array — an absent header yields [] where 4.6.1 returned null.

Workarounds

None for the data loss. For the uncaught exceptions, callers who cannot upgrade should wrap mail_json, mail_partial_json, headers_json and any X_raw access in a bare except Exception rather than catching only MailParserError subclasses.

References

  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf

items.content_html:
Patches

Fixed in 4.6.2. Upgrade with pip install --upgrade mail-parser.

Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching can tell them apart:

  • the first token of the from clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never a candidate;
  • an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;
  • a candidate must sit inside a ( / [ group;
  • IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;
  • the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing into sender-written headers.

The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the IPv6: tag and to prefer the longest valid form.

Behaviour change. get_server_ipaddress() now returns None rather than an unreliable value in two cases that previously returned an address: a from clause consisting of a bare address with no HELO marker (indistinguishable from EHLO <that address>), and a trusted hop naming no address at all. Callers must handle None.

Workarounds

None within mail-parser. Callers who cannot upgrade should not treat the return value of get_server_ipaddress() as trustworthy, and should derive sender attribution from an authenticated signal instead — the MTA's own logs, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC results computed outside this library.

items.content_html:
Summary

Two regular expressions used while parsing email headers backtrack polynomially on attacker-controlled input. Parsing a single small, well-formed email can consume minutes to hours of CPU, denying service to any process that parses untrusted mail.

Both are reachable from an ordinary parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes() or parse_from_file() call — no special API, option, or malformed structure is required by the victim.

Details

1. Address-header fallback regex (src/mailparser/utils.py)

get_addresses() falls back to _ADDR_FALLBACK_RE whenever email.utils.getaddresses(strict=True) yields no usable address. The alternative ([^<,]*?)\s*<([^>]+)> overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent \s* — a space matches both. Driven by finditer, which retries at every offset and rescans the remainder, matching degrades to quadratic on < padding and cubic on whitespace padding.

The fallback engages on the feature's own happy path, e.g. From: alice@example.com <bob@example.com>.

Measured (4.6.0, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64; reproduced identically on Linux and on CPython 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13):

Padding Parse time
valid address + 750 sp 0.38 s
+ 1500 sp 2.97 s
+ 3000 sp 23.4 s (×7.9/2×)
+ 6 KB sp 185 s
~100 KB sp hours

Fully RFC 5322-compliant folded headers (all lines ≤ 71 octets) trigger the same blowup, so the input passes normal MTA and library checks. ~100 KB of headers is within Postfix's default header_size_limit = 102400.

All six address headers parsed by the library (From, To, Cc, Bcc, Reply-To, Delivered-To) are affected and their cost adds up linearly.

2. Received-header clause splitter (src/mailparser/const.py)

parse_received() splits on _CLAUSE_SPLITTER, (?:^|\s+)(from|by|via|with|id|for|envelope-from)\s+. Under re.split this backtracks quadratically over any whitespace run that is not followed by a clause keyword. The pre-existing normalization collapsed only [\t\n], so literal spaces — including folded-header padding — reached the splitter intact.

Measured: 24 000 spaces in one Received: header → 22 s; ~100 KB → minutes.

Impact

Availability. A handful of small emails keeps every parsing worker of a mail gateway, ticketing system, quarantine UI, or archiving pipeline permanently busy. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

Anyone who parses email they did not author is affected — which is the library's purpose.

Patches

Fixed in 4.6.1.

  • The address fallback is now a linear scan: the header is split into comma-separated items (quote-aware, in Python), then each item is matched against a bounded angle-address <([^<>\s]+)> with the display name derived in Python, falling back to a bare-email match. Each pattern has a single non-nested quantifier over a negated character class → O(n). 2000 padding spaces: 3.5 s → <0.01 s. 256 KB padding: hours → 0.087 s. Output is preserved on every previously supported shape.
  • parse_received() collapses whitespace runs to a single space before splitting, so the splitter's \s+ only ever matches one character → O(n). The date is extracted from the raw header beforehand, so date formatting is unaffected. 24 000 spaces: 22 s → 0.003 s; 200 000 spaces: 0.004 s.

Regression tests assert linear-time behaviour for both paths.

Workarounds

None within the library. Upgrade to 4.6.1.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should cap total header size before parsing and enforce a wall-clock timeout around each parse.

References

  • https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-r7w7-vpq8-c5vv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129295

items.content_html:
A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

  • Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.
  • Validation that all output paths remain within the intended destination directory.
  • Rejection of symbolic link targets.
  • Normalization of Windows and POSIX path separators.
  • Validation and rejection of invalid or unsafe filenames.
  • Protection applied consistently in both write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

Users are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the patched release.

Credits

The vulnerability was responsibly reported by Niranjan Ganesan (Security Insights, https://securityinsights.io/, GitHub: @iam-niranjan).

The vulnerability was analyzed, remediated, and the security fix was implemented by Fedele Mantuano, maintainer of mail-parser (LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/fmantuano/).

mail-parser would like to thank Niranjan Ganesan for following a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process and for collaborating throughout the remediation and verification of the fix.

items.content_html:
termux-sync restore trusts fields inside an untrusted backup manifest and uses them as the extraction destination without validation.

During restore, each archive entry is handled as:

src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent extract_archive(archive, src_dir, ...)

extract_archive opens the archive and runs tarfile.extract for every member with no path jail and no filter:

with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tf: for member in tf.getmembers(): tf.extract(member, dest_path, set_attrs=True)

There is no check that manifest "source" stays under an expected restore root, that tar members stay inside dest_path, or that backup_name used in temporary paths cannot contain ".." or separators.

Impact: A victim who restores a malicious backup (local, shared, or from a compromised GitHub/Google Drive storage backend) can have arbitrary files written anywhere the Termux user can write. Overwriting shell startup files or executable scripts leads to local code execution on later use.

Reproduction (benign markers only):

  1. Build a backup directory with home.tar.gz (members: proof filename + optional config names) and manifest.json.
  2. Set files.home.source to any path whose parent is the desired write directory (e.g. $HOME/dummy_for_parent so parent is $HOME).
  3. Run the same extract path the tool uses: src_dir = Path(source).parent; tarfile.extract each member into src_dir.
  4. Observe attacker-controlled files created under $HOME and under other chosen roots (config / shell-rc style overwrite).

Expected: restore only writes under fixed, validated roots; reject unsafe source values and members that resolve outside dest. Actual: write destination is fully controlled by manifest.source; proof files and overwrites appear outside any intended jail.

Fix direction:

  • Do not trust manifest "source" for extract roots; use fixed app-defined destinations
  • Sanitize backup_name (basename; reject ".." and separators)
  • Extract with tarfile filter="data" (or equivalent boundary checks) and refuse escape
  • Treat backups as untrusted input

Actual result (local marker-only reproduction):

PROOF path: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/PWNED_BY_TERMUX_SYNC_RESTORE.txt PROOF exists? True PROOF content: PWNED This file was written by a malicious termux-sync backup restore path. Root cause: manifest files.*.source controls extract destination.

*** VULN CONFIRMED: arbitrary write to $HOME ***

important.conf => secret=ATTACKER_CONTROLLED *** VULN CONFIRMED: overwrite under attacker-chosen root ***

.bashrc_sim shows injected: export ATTACKER=1 *** VULN CONFIRMED: startup-file style overwrite ***

Extract roots used: home -> parent($HOME/dummy_for_parent) = $HOME config -> parent(.../victim_sim/nested_dummy) = .../victim_sim

Reported and credited to Niranj R Mahaswar ( GitHub: @NiranjMahaswar )

References

  • https://github.com/djunekz/termux-sync/security/advisories/GHSA-259w-wmqg-fp76

items.content_html:
Summary

nltk.parse.dependencygraph.dot2img invokes the Graphviz dot executable without the trusted-execution guarantees that NLTK applies to its other native-tool wrappers. The function resolves dot by bare name and then runs the resolved absolute path with a raw subprocess.run, omitting the ownership/writability check and the loader-environment scrub that nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted provides. On a POSIX host, a local, unprivileged actor who can write to any group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's PATH can plant a trojan dot; when the victim later renders a DependencyGraph (for example in a Jupyter notebook, which auto-invokes _repr_svg_) or calls dot2img directly, the planted binary executes as the victim. The advisory GHSA-6hwm-xvph-95vm (CVE-2026-78680) addressed the same untrusted-search-path class for the Graphviz dot invoker in nltk/translate/api.py, but dot2img received only part of that remediation and remains exploitable.

Root Cause

NLTK's native-tool security model layers four defenses (documented in nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md): (1) find_binary refuses a current-working-directory-relative match; (2) resolve_trusted_executable verifies the resolved file is a regular file that no other unprivileged user can replace (private parent directories, owner is the user or root, no group/world write bit); (3) shell execution is refused; (4) safe_env scrubs loader and interpreter environment variables before exec. Layers 2, 3, and 4 are reached only through nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted. dot2img calls find_binary("dot") (layer 1 only), then executes the result with subprocess.run([dot_binary, ...]) and no env= argument. Layer 1 rejects only non-absolute matches, so an absolute path returned by the which search stage survives even when the file lives in a writable directory. Because dot2img never calls spawn_trusted, the ownership check and environment scrub never run.

nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:626   dot_binary = find_binary("dot")          # layer 1 only
nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:631   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # no trust check, no env=
nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:638   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # binary-format branch, same gap
nltk/internals.py:1034              if searching_bare_name and not os.path.isabs(path): continue  # skips only relative matches
nltk/translate/api.py:145           process = spawn_trusted(dot_binary, [f"-T{output_format}"], ...)  # hardened sibling

Impact

Prerequisites: a POSIX host on which the attacker is a local, unprivileged user (or code) able to write to a group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's PATH. This includes the commonly cited case of a Homebrew /usr/local/bin with drwxrwxr-x permissions, or a writable directory placed early on PATH. The attacker plants a trojan dot there. When the victim renders a DependencyGraph (notebook _repr_svg_ auto-invocation) or calls dot2img directly, the trojan executes as the victim, yielding arbitrary local code execution in the victim's account: a local privilege-escalation and lateral-movement primitive. Because the child environment is not scrubbed, loader-injection variables (for example LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_*, GCONV_PATH) also reach the child, providing an additional execution surface. No control over NLTK inputs is required.

Proof of Concept

Requires: POSIX host, an importable NLTK build from the affected tree, and Python 3. No third-party dependencies.

  1. Create a world-writable directory and write an executable dot script into it that drops a marker and emits fake SVG.
  2. Prepend that directory to PATH and run from a neutral working directory (so this is not the current-working-directory vector).
  3. Show that resolve_trusted_executable refuses the planted binary (so the hardened path would raise) while dot2img executes it.
import os, stat, tempfile, subprocess, sys
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
dot = os.path.join(d, "dot")
with open(dot, "w") as f:
    f.write("#!/bin/sh\ntouch " + os.path.join(d, "MARKER") + "\necho '<svg><!-- planted dot ran --></svg>'\n")
os.chmod(dot, 0o777)
os.chmod(d, 0o777)
os.environ["PATH"] = d + os.pathsep + os.environ["PATH"]
os.chdir("/")
from nltk.pathsec import resolve_trusted_executable
from nltk.parse.dependencygraph import dot2img
print("resolve_trusted_executable(planted dot):", resolve_trusted_executable(os.path.join(d, "dot")))
out = dot2img("digraph G { a -> b }")
print("dot2img stdout:", repr(out))
print("planted dot executed (marker created):", os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, "MARKER")))

resolve_trusted_executable(planted dot): None
dot2img stdout: '<svg><!-- planted dot ran --></svg>\n'
planted dot executed (marker created): True

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: On a shared POSIX host, a group/world-writable directory is present on the victim's PATH (for example a writable directory early on PATH, or a Homebrew /usr/local/bin with group-write). The attacker writes a trojan dot into it.
  2. Control: The attacker fully controls the contents of the planted dot file; no control over NLTK inputs is needed.
  3. Path: The victim renders a DependencyGraph (notebook display triggers _repr_svg_ at nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:209, which calls dot2img) or calls dot2img directly.
  4. Guard: find_binary("dot") applies layer 1 only (nltk/internals.py:1034), which discards a relative current-working-directory match but returns the attacker's absolute path from the which stage; dot2img never invokes resolve_trusted_executable (layer 2) or safe_env (layer 4), unlike the hardened sibling nltk/translate/api.py:145.
  5. Primitive: subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...) (nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:631 and :638) executes the untrusted absolute path with the full inherited environment.
  6. Result: Arbitrary local code execution as the victim, plus a loader-injection surface via the unscrubbed environment.

Bypass Evidence

Canonical prior advisory: GHSA-6hwm-xvph-95vm (CVE-2026-78680), "Uncontrolled search path when invoking the Graphviz 'dot' binary" (CWE-426/CWE-427), patched at >= 3.10.3. That remediation was two-part: a uniform layer-1 current-working-directory refusal in find_binary, and a routing of native-tool dot invocations through nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted (layers 2 and 4). Inspection of the current released tree (nltk 3.10.3) shows dot2img received the layer-1 change (the function was rewritten from a bare subprocess.run(["dot", ...]) to find_binary("dot") plus a run of the absolute path, with a CWE-426/427 comment at nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:622-625) but did NOT receive the spawn_trusted routing. The sibling nltk/translate/api.py:145 does route through spawn_trusted, and nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md lists Graphviz dot only under translate/api.py; dot2img is absent from the hardened-wrapper inventory. Attempts to invalidate the finding all failed: (a) the claim that the fix covers all dot resolution is refuted because layer 1 filters only non-absolute matches and dot2img never reaches layers 2/4; (b) the duplicate hypothesis is refuted by a negative control, planting ./dot in the working directory with none on PATH makes find_binary("dot") raise LookupError, so the prior fix's working-directory guard still fires and this is the distinct residual ownership/environment gap; (c) the "system dot shadows the trojan" objection is refuted because realistic exploitation prepends the writable directory on PATH or replaces a dot already living in a writable PATH directory; (d) both the text and binary format branches share the identical unguarded exec, so it is not format-specific. A fresh PoC on the examined tree confirms resolve_trusted_executable refuses the planted binary while dot2img executes it.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)
  • Package: nltk
  • Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3
  • Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, latest published release as of the review date; source tree VERSION == 3.10.3)
  • Fix status: 3.10.4

The dot2img function has invoked dot via a raw subprocess since well before the prior advisory. The prior advisory's spawn_trusted standardization routed only the sibling translate/api.py invoker through the trusted-execution chokepoint, so this residual gap in dot2img exists from at least that remediation release onward and remains present in the latest published release (3.10.3). Precise introduction and remediation boundaries below 3.10.3 could not be independently established in this environment (no git tags or release history in the checkout); the confirmed statement is that the latest published release is affected and no fix for dot2img exists.

Suggested Fix

Route dot2img's execution through nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted(dot_binary, ["-T%s" % t], input=...), mirroring the sibling nltk/translate/api.py, so that the ownership/writability check (layer 2) and the loader-environment scrub (layer 4) apply, and handle TrustError/OSError with the same refusal pattern used at nltk/translate/api.py:152-157. Apply the change to both the text-format and binary-format branches. Add Graphviz dot under nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py to the per-wrapper inventory in nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md so the second invoker is tracked. Interim mitigation without a code change: ensure no group/world-writable directory appears on the PATH of any account that renders NLTK dependency graphs, and install Graphviz in a directory writable only by the user or root.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: IN PROGRESS (fix on an open pull request, not yet on develop).

Two open pull requests carry a fix.

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured). Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (internals.java() refuses a binary that resolve_trusted_executable rejects, _java_child_env drops the loader environment and pins PATH, dependencygraph.dot2img runs through pathsec.spawn_trusted). Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_7mxv_7h3q_9324.py (on that PR); verdict on its head: FIXED (planted absolute java refused with TrustError; loader and JVM environment scrubbed).

PR: #3887 "Resolve every executed tool binary absolute-only: prover9/mace4, megam, tadm, java, hunpos (untrusted search path, CWE-426/427)", open; head 3ac1c5641 at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 16b1de8ee, the head on which the verdicts below were measured). Fix commits: 992884a02 (the JVM is resolved before spawning and spawned through spawn_trusted) and b002a7288 (dot is spawned through the trusted path in dependencygraph). The #3753 probe run against this head reports STATIC (the planted java is refused with LookupError before the trust guard is reached).

The probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe: VULNERABLE (java() executed a planted untrusted binary from a writable directory).

Release: none.

items.content_html:
Impact

A critical vulnerability was discovered in the SAML SSO implementation of Sentry. It was reported to us via Sentry's private bug bounty program.

The vulnerability allows an attacker to take over any user account by using a malicious SAML Identity Provider and another organization on the same Sentry instance. The victim email address must be known in order to exploit this vulnerability.

Self-hosted users are only vulnerable if the following conditions are met:

  • They have more than one organization configured (SENTRY_SINGLE_ORGANIZATION = False).
  • A malicious user has existing access and permissions to modify SSO settings for another organization in their multi-organization instance.

Patches

  • Sentry SaaS: The fix was deployed in April. No action is required.
  • Self-Hosted Sentry: If only a single organization is allowed (SENTRY_SINGLE_ORGANIZATION = True), then no action is needed. Sentry recommends upgrading to version 26.4.1 or higher.

Workarounds

User account-based two-factor authentication prevents an attacker from being able to complete authentication with a victim's user account. Organization administrators cannot do this on a user's behalf, this requires individual users to ensure 2FA has been enabled for their account.

Users can manage their two-factor authentication settings through Account Settings > Security page. For step-by-step details, please see the Sentry helpdesk article.

Resources

  • https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/pull/113720

Please note that this is distinct vulnerability from the similar https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/security/advisories/GHSA-7pq6-v88g-wf3w from 2025.

In lightning-ai/pytorch-lightning version 2.3.2, a vulnerability exists in the LightningApp when running on a Windows host. The vulnerability occurs at the /api/v1/upload_file/ endpoint, allowing an attacker to write or overwrite arbitrary files by providing a crafted filename. This can lead to potential remote code execution (RCE) by overwriting critical files or placing malicious files in sensitive locations.
